text: This term I treated Data Structures as my main focus since I was juggling a full-time job and only had a few evenings to study, and the pacing felt tighter because it was in the summer, but I actually appreciated the way the workload pushed me to stay on top of things. text: Data Structures in the middle of this heavy semester has felt like wading through a maze of abstractions, and I came in with a strong coding background but not much theory, so the conceptual explanations clicked more than the real-world tie-ins. The instructor can make tough ideas feel doable during lectures, but the examples were thin and mostly Python pseudocode, which left me craving concrete scaffolds I could actually reuse in a project. By week six I noticed my team and I ended up leaning on each other more than staff, trading quick clarifications after hours rather than getting timely feedback from the TA, which made the grading comments feel thorough yet mysteriously delayed—like, yes, they explained the errors in detail, but the turnaround always came after we’d hit the next deadline. A late-semester turning point hit when a data-structure design problem finally clicked only after we reworked the approach and discovered the assessment was fair but exhausting, as if every small win came with a new hurdle. I still get frustrated by the lag in feedback, but I’ll admit the core ideas aren’t entirely off base, and the course leaves you with a stubborn, practical sense of how to structure problems even if the road there was rough.

text: I’m in my first semester here, juggling a full-time job, and Data Structures felt like it was designed around stacked deadlines more than a steady pace, which made sticking to a study plan tricky. Overall, it’s been calm but uneven, with a few concrete quirks that keep me from feeling fully confident.

text: This course was a mixed grind for me as a returning student who feels a bit rusty, but I did have enough time at points to catch up before deadlines, which helped a little. The practical work felt more like busywork than real skills I could actually transport to a job, and the heavy focus on reports meant I spent ages polishing documents instead of understanding the network concepts in a usable way. The exam week sticks in my memory more for how fast the scores came back and how thin the explanations were than for any real insight, and the rubric felt vague enough that I wasn’t sure what counted as a good answer. I fell behind with attendance early on and only caught up near the deadlines, which didn’t do wonders for my confidence as a returning student trying to rebuild momentum. Collaboration expectations were murky, and I wish the course had clearer guidance on what the group work actually required beyond “coordinate with others.” One memorable week was the midterm covering routing tables, where I realized I mostly remembered the terms but not the nuance, which sums up the whole thing: a lot of rote content and a few moments that almost clicked, but not enough to feel like real readiness. Overall, I would not take it again, even though some parts did spark a shred of understanding.

text: I’m new to the discipline and learning the basics, and Data Structures felt like a real first hurdle that somehow also clicked in spots. The toolset was pretty usable once I remembered to save often, and I appreciated the quick online IDE for small practice tasks between evening sessions. The course felt like an introductory service course that assumed a bit more prior exposure than I had, which left me scrambling to keep up during the midweek crunch and wishing the pacing matched the shorter study windows I can fit after work. Grading felt oddly vague—the rubric never quite mapped to what showed up on the tests, and explanations for why a solution scored a certain way were thin, even as the scores came back fast. People helped each other a lot more than staff did in the forums, which was both supportive and a reminder that I had to fill some gaps myself. The prerequisite felt like it set a higher bar, so I compared it a lot to the easier prereq I started with, which colored how I viewed the whole thing. Still, I’d probably land an A after a curve if I keep grinding the core ideas in the evenings.

text: Taking Data Structures with Dr. Miller last term as my main focus course was a rough ride; the organization felt scattered, with weekly announcements that arrived late and deadlines that moved around more than a schedule change in a lab. The grading rubric seems vague, so I’m unsure if my C reflects understanding or just how the rubric scraped the main points, and feedback quality really varied by assignment. Peer discussion helped more than the official materials, and I remember one office-hours chat where a quirky example about a phishing flow clicked for me, but otherwise I wasn’t convinced the tools were friendly. I wouldn’t take it again, even though a few moments did stick. The tradeoffs nag at me: it built a few instincts, but the friction and the late-night platform headaches wore me down.

text: This Linear Algebra class in my last semester before graduation felt like it barely met me where I am—comfortable with proofs but not with systems work, and I kept thinking the prereqs assumed more background than the catalog promised. The peer discussion sessions were the real lifeline; I’d sit with a few classmates and suddenly the whole thing clicked, while the official slides felt serviceable but not memorable—just a stream of bullets that didn’t stick. The biggest strain was the timing of feedback: I’d hand in a matrix decomposition assignment and hear back after the next deadline, which left me chasing the critique instead of using it to improve, especially since I needed this for a specialization anyway. I remember an exam that leaned on a few tricks from the lectures and a couple of tricky problem setups, and I walked away frustrated that the grading quirks didn’t align with what was actually taught in discussion. Compared to another course from the same term, this one felt more about getting through the motions than building the intuition I hoped for, and that late-semester turning point left me with mixed feelings I’m still sorting out.

text: I took Linear Algebra in the summer term, right after another hard class, so I mostly relied on recordings and notes because I couldn’t always make the live sessions and still try to keep up. As someone new to the discipline, the pace felt compressed and the pacing didn’t align well with my own slow start—the slides were serviceable but not memorable, and I left wanting a bit more intuition rather than just definitions. The biggest piece that stuck was the grading vibe: the instructor I liked, but the explanations behind the scores were thin, and feedback came too late to actually help with the next assignment, which made it hard to adjust on the fly. I didn’t feel a clear sense of how to collaborate in groups either; the collaboration structure seemed vague, so I mostly did my own thing and hoped the rubric would catch what mattered. There were moments where the content clicked with a concrete example in a project, yet those moments were rare and didn’t quite bridge the overall struggle with motivation, so I’d recommend it only if you’re prepared and can tolerate the rough edges.
